title: What Is Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery?
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of what is continuous integration and continuous delivery? and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to what is continuous integration and continuous delivery?.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on what is continuous integration and continuous delivery?. Continuous integration validates changes frequently; continuous delivery keeps validated changes ready to release; continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying changes. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: What Is Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery? matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Continuous integration validates changes frequently; continuous delivery keeps validated changes ready to release; continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying changes. Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Continuous integration validates changes frequently; continuous delivery keeps validated changes ready to release; continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying changes. Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Continuous integration (CI)
items.text: Use a scoped token, validate request inputs and event payloads, check HTTP/error status, handle pagination and rate limits, and avoid logging credentials or unneeded private response data.

items.title: Continuous delivery (CD)
items.text: For continuous delivery (cd), state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Continuous deployment
items.text: For continuous deployment, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: CI/CD pipeline stages
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Differences between automated testing and automated deployment
items.text: Make the check deterministic and fail with a meaningful status when requirements are not met. Preserve reports where useful and configure required branch checks to match the checks the workflow actually emits.

content_blocks.code:
name: CI then package
on: [push, pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Replace with the repository test command"
  package:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Package only after tests pass"
content_blocks.expected_output: The `package` job runs only after `test` succeeds; replace the placeholder commands with the repository’s real test and packaging commands.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a non-production branch and inspect the job dependency graph. The echo command is a structure demonstration, not a real build.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the original workflow or remove the experiment after verifying the dependency.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to what is continuous integration and continuous delivery?. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain what is continuous integration and continuous delivery?, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Understand why automation belongs beside source control and how events become repeatable work.

content.task: Apply what is continuous integration and continuous delivery? to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Continuous integration validates changes frequently; continuous delivery keeps validated changes ready to release; continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying changes.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Continuous integration validates changes frequently; continuous delivery keeps validated changes ready to release; continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying changes. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Continuous integration validates changes frequently; continuous delivery keeps validated changes ready to release; continuous deployment automatically releases qualifying changes.
Treat the workflow as an event-driven automation graph: an event starts the run, jobs are scheduled, steps execute on runners, and the run records a result.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
